title: Values
lead: Values are the third of the seven ideas, and they cover what a group thinks matters most.

p: Values are shared ideas about what a group considers important, desirable or morally right. They guide behaviour and can underpin norms.
In plain words, values are the things a group cares about most.

writers.name: Functionalists
writers.says: argue that shared values help people cooperate and feel part of a community.

list: Fairness and inclusion are values, because they are principles that a school wants its pupils to accept.
Inclusion is the principle, and helping a new pupil to settle in is the behaviour that puts it into practice.
Valuing education is a value, because it is about what matters rather than about how to succeed.
School subjects can reflect values: PE the value of good health, History the value of national identity and Religion the value of morality.
A school that asks pupils to recycle and join a litter pick shows that it sees caring for the environment as important.
A school that expects respect for other people, including when pupils talk online, shows that it sees respect as important.

p: Define the term: Values are shared ideas about what a group considers important, desirable or morally right. They guide behaviour and can underpin norms.
Item link: Fairness and inclusion in the item are values because they are principles the school wants pupils to accept.
Explain with an example: Praising pupils who help a newcomer encourages a norm of helpful behaviour based on those values. Inclusion is the principle; helping the new pupil puts it into practice.
Theory link: Functionalists argue that shared values help people cooperate and feel part of a community.

quote.t: A school encourages pupils to include others and treat them fairly. Students who help a new pupil settle in are praised by teachers and classmates.
